subject: physics

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Short Answer Question 12 (printed p.130). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: a reversible process retraces the same equilibrium states so that both system and surroundings return to their starting condition, requires quasi-static and dissipation-free conditions, and is an idealisation; an irreversible process cannot be so retraced, and friction, free expansion and heat flow across a finite temperature difference are standard examples, with every real process being irreversible.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The reversible process
lines: A reversible process can be made
the same sequence of states, so
that at the end BOTH the system
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both the system AND the surroundings return, along the same states.
steps.why: The word "reversible" names a PATH property: not just that the system can go back, but that the whole path — including the surroundings — can be undone with no trace left.
common_mistakes: Saying only the system returns to its initial state — the surroundings must return as well.
Describing it as a process that simply "can happen backwards" without the same-states condition.

recall.must_convey: That a reversible process retraces the same states so that both the system and the surroundings return to their starting condition.

steps.memory_tip: Reversible needs BOTH back: system and surroundings, by the same path.

steps.label: The conditions for reversibility
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both conditions: quasi-static AND free of dissipation.
steps.why: Any finite speed or any dissipation leaves the system out of equilibrium at some instant, and that instant cannot be undone — so both conditions are needed together, not either alone.
common_mistakes: Naming only one condition (slow, or loss-free) and treating it as sufficient on its own.
Saying a reversible process is one that happens in practice — it is an idealisation, approached but never reached.

recall.must_convey: That a reversible process must be quasi-static and free of friction and other dissipation, making it an idealisation.

steps.memory_tip: Reversible is an ideal LIMIT: infinitely slow and with no losses at all.

lines: Once it has run, the system and
steps.margin_note: Third mark. It cannot be retraced without leaving some change behind.
steps.why: Irreversibility is defined as the FAILURE of the reversible condition — it is not a separate rule but simply what happens whenever a process is not quasi-static or not loss-free.
common_mistakes: Saying an irreversible process cannot happen at all — it happens; it is just the one that cannot be undone without a trace.
Describing it only by an example, without stating the general definition first.

recall.must_convey: That an irreversible process cannot be retraced without leaving some change behind.

steps.memory_tip: Irreversible = reversible's two conditions FAIL — not slow enough, or not loss-free.

steps.label: Examples
lines: expansion of a gas, and heat
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. At least two named examples, and the statement that all natural processes are irreversible.
steps.why: Naming real examples is what shows the definition has been understood, not just memorised — and stating that ALL natural processes are irreversible is the point the whole answer is building to.
common_mistakes: Giving only one example instead of naming more than one kind of irreversibility.
Implying that some real processes are actually reversible — none are; reversible is only ever an ideal limit.

recall.must_convey: That friction, free expansion and heat flow across a finite temperature difference are irreversible, and that every real process is irreversible.
accept: heat flow across a temperature difference

steps.memory_tip: Friction, free expansion, heat across a gap: three everyday ways a process becomes irreversible.

insider_note: Naming examples such as friction, free expansion and heat flow across a finite temperature difference earns the fourth mark; adding that ALL natural processes are irreversible is worth including alongside them.
